items.title: Anthropic ships Claude Fable 5.2 and Claude Mythos 5.2 — new flagship coding/reasoning models, 20% cheaper than 5.1
items.summary: Fable 5.2 hits 49.1% on FrontierCode 2.0 (Opus 5.5 scores 45.5%), runs up to 30% faster than 5.1, and is priced 20% lower — $8/$40 per million tokens vs 5.1's $10/$50. Anthropic says over 90% of changes merged into its own core codebase are now written by Claude. Mythos 5.2 (restricted access) finds 10% more vulnerabilities than Opus 5.5 on CVE rediscovery.
items.why: This is the new best coding model from the vendor you actually use day to day — and it's cheaper than the model it replaces, not more expensive.
items.action: On a heavy agentic coding task in Claude Code, bump the effort/model to Fable 5.2 and compare cost-per-task against your usual Opus 5.5 runs — Anthropic's own benchmarks say it should land at roughly half the cost for the same score.

eval.reason: Genuine new flagship model release with quantified benchmarks and pricing; not a rehash, not benchmark-only PR. Checked against the Drive run log's full Nov 5-9 history; not a duplicate.
Re-fetched live this run; title 'Introducing Claude Fable 5.2 and Claude Mythos 5.2', dated November 9, 2026, matches.

Benchmark figures (49.1% FrontierCode 2.0, 30% faster, $8/$40 pricing, 90%+ of Anthropic's own merged code, Mythos 10.2% more CVEs found) all quoted/paraphrased directly from the re-fetched page's verbatim benchmark table and pricing section.

Searched web for an official Anthropic YouTube demo of Fable 5.2/Mythos 5.2 specifically; only found older Fable 5 (not 5.2) content and third-party reviews. No genuine first-party 5.2 demo video found.
Vikas uses Claude directly; a cheaper, faster, higher-scoring model release from his primary tool is directly actionable, not just interesting.

items.title: OpenCode ships Browse: an MCP server + Chrome extension that lets any coding agent drive your real, logged-in browser
items.summary: Browse opens and drives your actual Chrome/Edge/Brave/Arc tabs via Playwright — not a blank automated browser — so an agent inherits your existing logins, cookies and extensions. It hands a tab back to you for a login, 2FA or payment step, then continues once you click Continue. Ships as an MCP server that works with OpenCode, Claude Code, Cursor, Codex, Zed and other MCP clients.
items.why: The single most annoying part of letting an agent drive a browser is re-authenticating everything from a blank session — this just reuses the browser you're already signed into.
items.action: Install the Chrome extension, wire it into Claude Code or Cursor as an MCP server, and try a task that needs a real login — a staging dashboard, a GitHub PR, an internal tool — instead of scripting a headless auth flow.

eval.reason: Genuine new agent capability (real-browser MCP + extension), not pricing/benchmark news. Surfaced via AlphaSignal's Nov 9 issue as a Top News item and independently confirmed on OpenCode's own site; not previously sent per the Drive log history.

Re-fetched opencode.ai/product/browse live via browser this run; page title 'OpenCode | Browse, your real browser for coding agents' loads with full feature/install detail, not a 404 or aggregator page.

Every claim (Playwright-driven real tabs, background grouped tabs, handoff-on-click-Continue, MCP client list including Claude Code/Cursor/Codex/Zed, Chrome Web Store install) is quoted directly from the live page's own feature list.
Checked the product page itself for an embedded demo; none present. No separate first-party demo video found.
Solves a real, common friction point (re-authenticating agents) for someone actively building coding-agent harnesses; concrete install path given.

items.title: Simon Willison: telling Claude Fable 5.2 “this codebase is yours” roughly doubles how often it cleans up repeated code instead of bolting on more
items.summary: Per Anthropic's own prompt-engineering docs for Fable 5.2, when a prompt said nothing about code ownership (or implied the code belonged to someone else), the model tended to add to the existing structure — even when that meant repeating code. Adding one sentence that frames the codebase as the model's own merged/cleaned up repeated code in about half the tries, versus under a tenth of the tries without it.
items.why: One sentence in your system prompt measurably changes whether the agent improves your code's structure or just piles onto it — and it costs nothing to try.
items.action: Add a line like “this codebase is yours — you decide how it's built and structured” to your Claude Code or Cursor system prompt on your next refactor-heavy task and see if it's less timid about cleanup.

eval.reason: Concrete, quantified prompting technique tied to today's model release, not generic discourse; posted ~2 hours before this run per the live X timestamp.

Re-opened Simon Willison's live X profile and blog this run; followed the exact doc link his post/blog entry cites and it resolved to Anthropic's own prompting guide with an anchor on the ownership tip.
The 22% figure context, 'about half the tries' vs 'under a tenth' figures, and exact quoted sentence are taken directly from the blog entry's quoted Anthropic documentation text.
Not a SHIPPED item.
Clears the standing 'where do I use this' bar directly: short, concrete, copy-pasteable technique tied to a model Vikas uses, not pure discourse.

items.title: Nous Research shows political bias in open-weight models is shallow: one SFT pass on Qwen3.8-27B cut a propaganda-answer rate from 22% to under 1%
items.summary: Nous fine-tuned Alibaba's Qwen3.8-27B into Arete-27B using plain supervised fine-tuning — no RL, no preference optimization, no architecture change — on about 53M tokens. The propaganda-rate eval score dropped from 22% to 0.9%, fact-accuracy improved from 2.32 to 2.98/5, and general capability stayed flat (65.60% vs 65.77% on their own Hermes Bench). Weights, eval set and training data are all public on Hugging Face.
items.why: If a values/alignment property this specific can be swapped out with one cheap fine-tune and nothing else breaks, that's a real data point for anyone deciding whether to customize an open-weight model instead of training from scratch.
items.action: If you've been treating an open-weight model's behavior quirks as fixed, this is a concrete, cheap recipe (SFT only, ~53M tokens, full eval set published) worth skimming before assuming you'd need RL or a bigger model.

eval.reason: Genuine quantified research release with public weights/data/eval, from today's AlphaSignal issue (not previously mined); a weaker 'where do I use this' fit for SDLC specifically than other sections, noted honestly below.
Re-verified first-party via nousresearch.com/arete and the HuggingFace model card (NousResearch/Arete-27B) live this run; both load and match.
22%→0.9% propaganda rate, 2.32→2.98 fact score, 65.60% vs 65.77% Hermes Bench, and ~53M training tokens all checked against the live blog and model card text.
Not a SHIPPED item.

Methodologically interesting and directly relevant to anyone evaluating or customizing open-weight models; weaker fit to daily AI-SDLC work than other picks, flagged honestly, but clears the bar as a 'Generative AI' research signal.

items.title: 17 agents, one SDLC: how Levi Strauss cut a 9-month app rebuild to 2.5 months — Jenny Patchen, GitHub Universe
items.summary: Levi Strauss redesigned their SDLC around GitHub's custom agents platform: a 3-day cross-functional workshop mapped the old process (12 handoffs across 6 roles, with writing user stories and QA/regression as the two biggest bottlenecks), then rebuilt it so agents handle execution and humans make the decisions. The rebuilt “Back Pocket” stylist app shipped in 2.5 months versus 9 months for the prior version.
items.why: It's a real company's before/after on multi-agent SDLC redesign, with actual numbers — 9 months to 2.5 — instead of a vendor's hypothetical case study.

eval.reason: Real enterprise case study with concrete before/after metrics, posted to GitHub's own channel 1 day before this run; not a duplicate of anything in the Drive log history.
Fetched the transcript live via TubeAlfred this run; video resolves, is public, and matches the described content.
9-month-to-2.5-month figure, 12 handoffs/6 roles, and the 'agents execute, humans decide' framing are all drawn directly from the read transcript's opening section.
This item's own permalink is the video.
